how hard your sliders steer Every ranking in the app is a weighted average of eleven axes, and most frames average about the same — so on flat the top of the field sits inside a tenth of a point and your priorities cannot show. Each step up gives the sliders you raised more of the verdict. where the frame scores come from Physics mode recomputes every frame from its own published specs — recoil weight from the parallel axis theorem, spin from strings per square inch, power from stiffness and the beam profile (average depth plus taper — 23/26/23 is not a constant 26). Serve, smash and slice go blank: they trade racket speed against effective mass, or they belong to your hand, and no honest formula reaches them. The two views disagree on purpose — that disagreement is itself the interesting number.

self-rating department · NTRP
The other half of the equation: not what the gear can do, but what you can do. Ten axes from the USTA NTRP characteristics, each with a drill that earns the score, resolve into a bracket — and into a target for the nineteen sliders on the racket and string benches. Nothing is applied until you press the button.

Scores map linearly: NTRP = 2.00 + 0.25 × weighted mean, so 4 = 3.0, 6 = 3.5, 8 = 4.0, 10 = 4.5. An axis you have not measured is capped at 8 — a 4.5 has to be earned on court, not felt. Sessions live in this browser; export the log if you want it to outlive a cleared cache.

Slider suggestion — what this profile asks of the gear

Ten player axes, each carrying its own weight, resolve into a target for your priority sliders — eleven on the racket side, eight on the string side. The stance decides what the profile does with a score: compensate lets weaknesses pull the gear, amplify lets strengths pull it. Sync my priorities writes these nineteen numbers into your nineteen priority sliders — the same sliders the spin-first and arm-first presets set, and the only thing it touches. Your frames, your customs and “my feel” rows, your shelves and your intro answers all stay exactly as they are; what changes is how they are weighed, so the rankings, medals and setups re-sort at once. It then stays synced: from that moment the stance moves both sets of sliders live, and you can watch the shortlist follow. Click to unlink ends that following and leaves the sliders standing exactly where they are — nothing is restored, nothing is undone; they are simply yours to drag by hand again.

The protocol — what earns a score

Every axis has one drill and five pass marks. Run it, count, set the score, then flip the axis to measured. Until you do, the axis stays an estimate and is capped at 8 in the calculation.

What the number is worth elsewhere

NTRP → UTR

No official conversion exists. These are observed crossover ranges, not a formula. Anything under 3.0 sits below the published data and carries a † in the readout.

Germany — Leistungsklasse

NTRP is a US league label; in Munich the currency is the DTB LK, running from LK 1.0 (elite) to LK 25.0.

Adults start around LK 24.0. Only wins move it — losses cost nothing. You need club membership and a DTB-ID, then it updates weekly.

One season of Medenspiele or LK tournaments gives you a hard number that everyone you actually meet on court understands.

The match test

Ratings are relational. Borrow someone else's calibrated number and play sets against it.

vs. a known 4.0: 0–2 games per set → 3.0–3.5 · 3–4 games → solid 3.5 · splitting sets or winning breakers → 4.0.

Practice strokes flatter. The scoreboard doesn't.

where these numbers come from — and where they stop

1 · The specs are published figures. Weight, head size, string pattern, RA stiffness, swingweight, balance and beam come from the manufacturers. They are nominal values with real production spread — strung versus unstrung, and ±7 g is ordinary on a frame. A data sheet is not a scale.

2 · The 1–10 axis values are a disclosed rule, not measurements. No laboratory outputs “spin 9/10”. Every frame on this bench is scored from its own specs by one published rule, the same for all of them, and you can switch to pure physics in the gear menu to see the stricter version:

  • Recoil weight — Icm = SW − M × (balance − 10 cm)², the parallel axis theorem. How hard the frame is to push back at impact. Two frames can share a swingweight and differ by 40 kg·cm² here, and that is what you feel blocking a fast return.
  • Manoeuvrability — inverse swingweight. Stability and return — recoil weight.
  • Spin — strings per square inch, not the raw pattern: the same 16×19 on a bigger head slides and snaps back further.
  • Power — stiffness, the beam profile and head size. The beam enters as its average depth plus its taper (max − min of the published section, e.g. 23/26/23 → avg 24, taper 3): a hoop that is 26 mm only at mid-hoop is softer than 26 mm everywhere, and the taper itself is the power/aero geometry. Control is its counterpart, not an independent number.
  • Comfort — inverse stiffness. Precision — head size.

3 · Three axes have no formula, and physics mode leaves them blank. Serve and smash trade racket speed against effective mass and cannot be resolved from static specs; slice and touch belong to the player's hand. A number there would be invented, so there is a dash instead.

4 · No third-party lab database is used. Every figure above is computed from the frame's own published specs. One quantity stays out of reach without measurement: twistweight, the resistance to twisting on an off-centre hit. Manufacturers do not publish it, so this tool does not claim it.

Inertial method: Rod Cross, Customising a tennis racket, University of Sydney · Howard Brody, The Physics and Technology of Tennis. Player axes follow the USTA NTRP General Characteristics — the wording, not the rating: a real NTRP is issued by the USTA from match results, and a UTR is computed by Universal Tennis from up to 30 matches in twelve months. Neither can be produced by a self-assessment, and this tool does not produce one.

Log a customization

Tell the bench what you did — lead tape, grip build-up, a different butt cap. Give it the new numbers and the frame is re-scored from them.
what you can actually do — and what it moves
Lead at 10 & 2 — swingweight up roughly a point per gram: plow-through, power and stability climb; maneuverability drops and difficulty creeps up.
Lead at 12 (the tip) — the strongest swingweight gain per gram: depth and stability rise most, fast exchanges get hardest.
Lead at 3 & 9 — twist resistance: off-center hits calm down and feel steadies, with only a small swingweight rise.
Silicone or lead in the handle — mass rises but balance pulls toward the hand: feel, comfort and stability climb while the frame stays quick.
Overgrip build-up — a few grams at the very bottom: headlight, whippier through contact, the scores barely move.
The estimator reads three numbers — weight, swingweight, balance — but you can simply write what you did in words: “6 g lead at 12”, “silicone in the handle”. The panel reads the grams and the placement, works the numbers out with the standard mass-placement math, fills the fields above, and the preview re-scores instantly. Type your own numbers any time — they always win over the derived ones.
Customized frames keep their own row and show a customized chip; hover it to read what was done.

Until then a † means the figure is calculated rather than measured. Solinco Conf. Soft × Head Lynx Tour is the other court-tested row: liked, but clearly below it, and the field gap matches the index gap. Queued next: the 1.30 Solinco Mach 10 gauge step, then a full bed of ReString Zero, then ReString Zero 1.28 × Sync 1.23. Cells marked † are re-derived for this rebuild rather than carried from the original bench — overwrite them freely. Babolat RPM Blast × Touch VS gut is the only natural-gut bed here — it sets the ceiling on feel and arm friendliness, at the cost of price and a poly-saws-gut lifespan. Note the pull between axes: raising tension toward 25/23 kg lifts control but pushes every row down the arm column.

The model, and where it comes from — four findings from published racquet science The model, and where it comes from. Four findings from published racquet science drive every score here. 1 · Shock compounds. Frame stiffness (RA) and string-bed dynamic stiffness add up into one system; impact-shock work at Tennis Warehouse University and in Rod Cross & Crawford Lindsey's Technical Tennis / The Physics and Technology of Tennis shows a stiff frame strung with a stiff poly transfers the most shock to the arm — so the calibrator rewards soft-in-stiff and flexible-frame-with-poly pairings and flags stiff-on-stiff. 2 · Spin is snapback. High-speed TWU studies traced most spin to the mains sliding sideways and snapping back; slick co-polys do this best, and a dense 18×20 pattern — which pinches that movement — gains the most from them, while open patterns add bite to almost anything. 3 · The power budget is shared. A launchy frame plus a lively bed overshoots; a muted frame plus a board of a bed plays dead. The calibrator scores the sum of frame power and string power against a middle band, which is why control polys top the list in powerful frames and livelier beds float up in low-powered ones. 4 · Patterns eat strings. Open patterns let strings move more, so thin or heavily shaped beds wear fastest exactly where they bite hardest — the longevity penalty you'll see on some pairings. The classic exceptions are priced in too: natural-gut hybrids as the historic arm-saver in stiff frames, poly mains for spin control in everything modern. Tensions are read as filed per bed; in a stiff-on-stiff system, dropping 1–2 kg buys back comfort before any string change does.
